terms.gloss: push oneself up on one’s arms: do a push-up
terms.grammar: sublevō, sublevāre, sublevāvī, sublevātum, with the reflexive; bracchiīs, ablative of means; identidem for a set
evidence: Caes. BG 6.27: neque, sī quō adflīctae cāsū concidērunt, ērigere sēsē aut sublevāre possunt
terms.comment: A description of ours: we have found no word for a push-up in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini. Sublevāre is to lift from beneath, and sē sublevāre to raise oneself, as Caesar says of the elk that cannot get up once it has fallen. For a set, add identidem, as Traupman does for sit-ups (identidem residēre, Traupman 65). Latin says it with a verb.

phrases.latin: Prōnus humī jacē; deinde tē bracchiīs identidem sublevā.
phrases.english: Lie face down on the floor; then push yourself up on your arms, again and again.
How many push-ups can you do? — Ten!

sources: Lewis & Short: sublevo · Lewis & Short: bracchium · Lewis & Short: identidem
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 65.
